Shipping companies also had to acquire suitable vessels, while exporters altered packing and scheduling. Standardisation coordinated these investments; it did not replace them. The distinction matters because it prevents an object from receiving sole credit for a change produced by an entire system.

rows.sourceExcerpt: Shared dimensions solve a compatibility problem, not a structural one. A damaged box can endanger workers and cargo even if it fits every crane. International coordination therefore includes safety and inspection requirements as well as measurements. An inspection regime makes visible who must check condition and when. rows.sourceExcerpt: A container standard does not decide which goods should move, how emissions should be priced or whether a route is socially desirable. Those questions remain outside the box. Policy must still consider external costs, labour transitions and the resilience of long supply chains.

rows.sourceExcerpt: Lock-in is not paralysis. Operators can introduce tracking devices, improved seals or new inspection methods without discarding the entire interface. responseBinding.questionText: The author describes the container as institutional because it

rows.sourceExcerpt: The container is best understood as an institutional object. Its steel walls carry goods, while its standard form carries commitments among organisations that may never meet. Those commitments reduce uncertainty at each transfer and make large-scale scheduling possible. They also distribute dependence: a delay in one port can propagate through many routes. The achievement of standardisation is therefore neither the triumph of a clever box nor a tale of rigid uniformity. It is the construction of a shared platform whose benefits and constraints must be governed over time.

responseBinding.questionText: What must be moved before the visit?

bindings.audiblePhrase: The ladder can stay where it is, but I need to move the plant pots. They are the only things blocking the working area.

responseBinding.questionText: What will the inspector measure first?

bindings.audiblePhrase: Good. The inspector will begin by measuring the sediment depth at the bottom. The screen check and water sample come afterwards, so the tank should not be emptied.

responseBinding.questionText: What should remain switched off?

bindings.audiblePhrase: The timer can remain as it is, but please keep the garden pump switched off from breakfast until the inspection has finished.

responseBinding.questionText: Where will the water sample be taken?

bindings.audiblePhrase: We need a household sample, so it will be taken from the kitchen tap, not the outdoor tank tap. The technician will call ten minutes before arrival.

responseBinding.questionText: Why must stallholders arrive during their allocated unloading window?
responseBinding.correctOptionText: to keep the shared lane moving

bindings.audiblePhrase: Your coloured pass shows an unloading time. Please keep to it, not because the pitch changes or the parking is cheaper, but because one shared lane must keep moving.

responseBinding.questionText: What will staff check before electrical equipment is used?

bindings.audiblePhrase: At the power desk, staff do not count appliances or judge cable colour. They check that each powered item carries a current power tag before it is connected.

responseBinding.questionText: What is the main purpose of the grey waste station?

bindings.audiblePhrase: The grey station is for tied bags of general non-food rubbish. Cardboard goes to the reuse cage, while cooking oil has its own sealed return point.

responseBinding.questionText: What happens at the quiet close?
responseBinding.correctOptionText: music stops before final sales end

bindings.audiblePhrase: At nine forty-five we begin the quiet close. Trading continues for fifteen minutes, but amplified music stops so nearby residents are not disturbed.

responseBinding.questionText: Which document must be displayed at every stall?

bindings.audiblePhrase: A vehicle pass only admits you to unloading, and prices are your responsibility. The laminated stall permit must remain visible throughout the evening.

responseBinding.questionText: Where should empty delivery crates be taken?

bindings.audiblePhrase: Once unloaded, collapse empty delivery crates and take them back to the loading bay. Do not leave them behind your stall.

responseBinding.questionText: Where are damaged extension leads reported?

bindings.audiblePhrase: If an extension lead is split or its tag cannot be read, carry it unplugged to the power desk and report it there.

responseBinding.questionText: Where should tied rubbish bags go?

bindings.audiblePhrase: Tie ordinary rubbish securely. Those bags belong at the grey waste station, not at the cardboard cage beside it.

responseBinding.questionText: Where is cooled cooking oil returned?

bindings.audiblePhrase: Let used oil cool in its original covered container. Return it only at the oil return point after the dinner rush.

responseBinding.questionText: Where can a lost permit be reprinted?

bindings.audiblePhrase: If wind damages your permit or you misplace it, the permit office can verify your booking and print a replacement.

responseBinding.questionText: What problem do the students identify in their first design?

bindings.audiblePhrase: Our first plan compares the woodland and sports field as if habitat is the only difference, but the woodland plots are much wetter. Soil moisture could explain a count difference.

responseBinding.questionText: Why do they retain mustard extraction?

bindings.audiblePhrase: I considered hand sorting alone, yet effort would vary. We should retain mustard extraction because we can apply the same concentration, area and waiting time at every plot.

responseBinding.questionText: How will they reduce observer bias?
responseBinding.correctOptionText: the same pair will sort every sample

bindings.audiblePhrase: For observer bias, swapping guides will not help. The same pair of people should sort every sample, then resolve disagreements together.

responseBinding.questionText: What will be recorded before extraction begins?

bindings.audiblePhrase: Before any solution is poured, we will record soil moisture. Worm length and vegetation height can be secondary, but moisture must come first.

responseBinding.questionText: Which comparison becomes their primary analysis?

bindings.audiblePhrase: So the primary comparison will use paired moist plots, one in each habitat. Total habitat counts and time-of-day patterns can remain exploratory.

responseBinding.questionText: Different recent rainfall

bindings.audiblePhrase: Recent rainfall creates unequal moisture. Pairing plots by their measured moisture is the revision that addresses that problem.

responseBinding.questionText: Unequal extraction duration

bindings.audiblePhrase: If one team waits five minutes and another waits ten, effort changes. We will standardise extraction time with a single timer.

responseBinding.questionText: Disagreement over juvenile specimens

bindings.audiblePhrase: Juvenile worms are hard to identify consistently. A shared identification check by both students should reduce disagreement.

responseBinding.questionText: Uncertain species record

bindings.audiblePhrase: When a specimen remains uncertain, we will photograph it against a scale and confirm it later rather than inventing a species label.

responseBinding.questionText: Trampling before the survey

bindings.audiblePhrase: To prevent trampling from changing the surface, we will measure each quadrat before sampling and approach from the marked path.

responseBinding.questionText: A downward ______ contains a broad range of frequencies.

bindings.audiblePhrase: Many bats emit a downward frequency sweep, so a single brief call carries a broad range of frequencies rather than one unchanging note.

responseBinding.questionText: Distance is inferred from the ______ between call and echo.

bindings.audiblePhrase: The simplest ranging cue is echo delay: the interval between the outgoing call and its return increases with target distance.

responseBinding.questionText: A structure called the ______ helps analyse returning sound.

bindings.audiblePhrase: In the outer ear, a small projection called the tragus contributes cues that help the auditory system analyse returning sound.

responseBinding.questionText: Calls may be timed in relation to each ______.

bindings.audiblePhrase: During flight, call production may be coordinated with each wingbeat, which can reduce the energetic cost of breathing and calling.

responseBinding.questionText: Dense vegetation creates a ______ habitat.

bindings.audiblePhrase: Branches and leaves make what researchers call a cluttered habitat, where echoes arrive from many surfaces in very quick succession.

responseBinding.questionText: Near objects require ______ calls.

bindings.audiblePhrase: When a bat approaches vegetation, shorter calls reduce overlap between an outgoing signal and the earliest returning echoes.

responseBinding.questionText: What physical feature may be counted to estimate clutter?

bindings.audiblePhrase: One practical clutter measure is to count vegetation gaps along a defined line, although other optical and spatial measures are possible.

responseBinding.questionText: What must a bat separate from prey echoes?

bindings.audiblePhrase: To detect an insect near foliage, the bat must separate the prey echo from strong background echoes returned by leaves and stems.

responseBinding.questionText: What movement can change the direction of reception?

bindings.audiblePhrase: Small ear movement can change the direction from which sound is received most strongly, adding dynamic information during approach.

responseBinding.questionText: What benefit do brief calls provide near obstacles?

bindings.audiblePhrase: In dense vegetation, the chief benefit of brief calls is rapid updates about nearby obstacles. Their lower energy can shorten range, but that is a cost rather than the benefit.
